title: Design a Vending Machine
summary: The canonical State pattern question. It is asked because the naive version — a pile of booleans and nested ifs — works, and then falls apart the moment someone presses refund at the wrong moment.

evidence.title: Design a vending machine system
evidence.note: A multi-location variant: customers order through a central platform and collect at a chosen machine.

evidence.title: Amazon interview experience — SDE-2
evidence.quote: Design a vending machine with following functionalities - Three types of Users : User, Operator, Admin - User can select and buy multiple items at a time.

blocks.title: What you are actually being asked
blocks.text: This is a **State pattern** question and the interviewer knows you know that. What they are actually watching is whether you can say *why* — that the same input means different things depending on where the machine is, and that encoding that in booleans produces an `if` ladder nobody can extend.

A machine holds products in slots. A customer inserts coins or notes, selects a product, and the machine either dispenses it with change, or refuses and refunds. It must never dispense without payment, and never keep money without dispensing.

items.title: Which denominations, and can it always make change?
items.text: A machine that cannot make exact change has to refuse the sale *before* taking the money. This is the requirement that catches people out.

items.title: Can a customer cancel mid-transaction?
items.text: Yes, always. It is the transition that breaks boolean-based designs, which is exactly why they ask.

items.title: One product per transaction, or several?
items.text: Assume one unless told otherwise, and say you are assuming it.

items.title: Who refills it, and is that a separate role?
items.text: An operator interface is a nice scope boundary — mention it, keep it out unless asked.

items.title: What happens on a power cut mid-dispense?
items.text: Almost always out of scope, but naming it shows you think about partial failure.

blocks.filename: The version that gets you cut

items: Four booleans is sixteen combinations, of which perhaps five are legal — and nothing in the code says which.
The rule *“cancel is legal while collecting money but not while dispensing”* is nowhere; it is an emergent property of the ordering.

blocks.title: Five states, and every transition is a method
blocks.caption: `HasMoney` is the only state that accepts a cancel refund. That rule is now a property of one class instead of a condition scattered across a ladder.
blocks.code:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> HasMoney : insertCoin()
    Idle --> Idle : select() / reject "insert money"
    HasMoney --> HasMoney : insertCoin()
    HasMoney --> Idle : cancel() / refund all
    HasMoney --> Dispensing : select() / funds ok, stock ok, change ok
    HasMoney --> HasMoney : select() / insufficient or no change
    Dispensing --> ReturningChange : product released
    ReturningChange --> Idle : change returned
    Idle --> OutOfService : stockEmpty() or coinJam()
    OutOfService --> Idle : refill()

blocks.title: Class design
blocks.caption: The machine holds a state object and delegates. It contains no `if` about what is currently happening.
blocks.code:
classDiagram
    class VendingMachine {
        -State state
        -Inventory inventory
        -CoinBox coins
        -int credit
        +void insert(Coin c)
        +void select(String code)
        +void cancel()
        +void setState(State s)
    }
    class State {
        <<interface>>
        +void insert(VendingMachine m, Coin c)
        +void select(VendingMachine m, String code)
        +void cancel(VendingMachine m)
    }
    class Inventory {
        -Map~String, Slot~ slots
        +boolean available(String code)
        +Product release(String code)
    }
    class CoinBox {
        -Map~Coin, Integer~ held
        +boolean canMakeChange(int amount)
        +List~Coin~ dispenseChange(int amount)
    }
    State <|.. IdleState
    State <|.. HasMoneyState
    State <|.. DispensingState
    State <|.. OutOfServiceState
    VendingMachine --> State
    VendingMachine o-- Inventory
    VendingMachine o-- CoinBox

blocks.title: Check change before releasing the product
blocks.text: Release first and you have handed over a drink you cannot give change for. The order — verify stock, verify funds, **verify change**, then release — is the correctness argument, and stating it unprompted is worth more than the pattern.

blocks.title: Why State beats an enum plus a switch
blocks.text: An enum with a `switch` is the same logic with worse locality: adding a state means finding every `switch` in the file. With a class per state, adding `CardPaymentState` is a new file and one transition. Say that; it is the answer to *“why not just an enum?”*

blocks.title: The qualifier is the point
blocks.text: *“Greedy works because these denominations are canonical; for an arbitrary set I would need the coin-change DP.”* Interviewers ask this exact follow-up. Volunteering it is free credit.
One physical machine has one customer, so this is usually out of scope — say that, then say what changes if it is not:

items: The Netflix-style variant, where orders arrive through a central platform, is genuinely concurrent: two customers can reserve the last can.
Stock decrement must be atomic with the sale, or the machine oversells.
The state object itself becomes shared mutable state. Per-machine locking is fine; a global lock across machines is not.

items.title: Add card payment
items.text: A new state, or a `PaymentMethod` strategy the money-collecting state delegates to. Both defensible; pick one and say why.

items.title: Support multiple items in one transaction
items.text: Credit stops being consumed by one selection, so `HasMoney` gains a basket. The state machine shape does not change, which is the point.

items.title: Refill and audit by an operator
items.text: A separate interface and an `OutOfService` transition. Worth noting the operator must not be able to trigger a dispense.

items.title: The machine cannot make change
items.text: Refuse before accepting, display “exact change only”, and reject coins that would create unchangeable credit.

items.title: Central platform, many machines
items.text: The Netflix variant. Stock becomes a distributed reservation, and the machine is now a consumer of an order queue rather than the source of truth.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state before you are asked

items: Select before inserting money → rejected in `IdleState`, no credit touched.
Cancel while dispensing → ignored. The `Dispensing` state simply has no `cancel` behaviour, which is the pattern doing its job.
Exact money, zero change → must not call the change machinery at all.
Sold out after selection but before dispense → only possible in the concurrent variant; the reservation is what prevents it.
Coin inserted while out of service → returned immediately, never banked.

rows: Explains that the same input means different things per state
A behaviour that only one state has
A new state class and one transition

blocks.title: The 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0–5** clarify denominations, cancel, change. **5–10** show the boolean version and kill it. **10–16** draw the state diagram. **16–32** code `State`, `Idle`, `HasMoney`, and the dispense path. **32–38** change-making with the greedy caveat. **38–45** card payment or the multi-machine variant.
